note: Practice questions (Claude-drafted, original wording) for C1 and C2, 300 per level, written to the CEFR scope of each level (advanced grammar, collocation and idiom, and argumentative academic reading in the style of advanced English exams). Imported as drafts for teacher review.

passages.C1P_MEMORYPALACE: The 'memory palace' is a technique dating back to ancient Greece. To use it, you imagine a familiar building and mentally place the items you want to remember in specific locations along a route through it. Later, by walking through the building in your mind, you retrieve the items in order. Memory champions routinely use the method to memorise long sequences of numbers or cards. Researchers have found that ordinary people trained in the technique for several weeks show marked improvements in recall, and that these gains can persist for months.
passages.C1P_GIGHISTORY: The notion that a 'job for life' was once the norm is, according to economic historians, something of a myth. While many workers in the mid-twentieth century did remain with a single employer for decades, large sections of the workforce — particularly women, migrants and those in agriculture — experienced insecure and seasonal work throughout. What has changed, they argue, is less the existence of precarious work than its spread into professions that were previously regarded as secure.
passages.C1P_URBANHEAT: Cities are typically several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofs absorb heat during the day and release it at night, while the lack of vegetation reduces cooling through evaporation. As heatwaves become more frequent, planners are experimenting with reflective roofing materials, street trees and 'pocket parks'. Such measures can lower local temperatures significantly, though their effectiveness depends on being implemented at scale.
passages.C1P_MULTITASK: Despite the widespread belief that multitasking boosts productivity, research consistently suggests otherwise. What we experience as doing several things at once is usually rapid switching between tasks, and each switch carries a cost in time and accuracy. Heavy multitaskers, studies indicate, are often worse at filtering out irrelevant information. Nevertheless, some combinations — such as listening to music while performing a routine physical task — appear to cause little interference, because they draw on different mental resources.
passages.C1P_PLACEBO: The placebo effect — improvement in a patient's condition after receiving a treatment with no active ingredient — is one of the most intriguing phenomena in medicine. Remarkably, some studies have found that placebos can work even when patients are told they are taking an inactive pill. Researchers believe that expectations and the ritual of treatment trigger real changes in the brain, particularly in the perception of pain. However, placebos have little effect on the underlying causes of serious diseases, which is why their use outside research raises ethical questions.
passages.C1P_HERITAGELANG: Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today, linguists estimate that around half may disappear by the end of the century. When a language dies, it is not only words that are lost but also knowledge about local plants, medicine and history encoded in it. Revitalisation efforts have had notable successes: Welsh, for instance, has seen a rise in speakers thanks to bilingual education and broadcasting. Yet such efforts depend heavily on the commitment of communities themselves; government policy alone is rarely sufficient.
passages.C1P_MINIMALISM: Minimalism, the practice of deliberately owning fewer possessions, has attracted a devoted following. Its advocates claim that decluttering reduces stress and frees up time and money for experiences rather than objects. Sceptics, however, point out that minimalism is often marketed as a lifestyle product in itself, complete with expensive 'essential' items and books. They also note that choosing to own little is a privilege available mainly to those who could afford to replace things if needed.
passages.C1P_CROWDFUND: Crowdfunding platforms allow creators to raise money directly from the public, bypassing banks and traditional investors. Many projects, from board games to documentaries, owe their existence to such campaigns. However, backers are not investors in the usual sense: they usually receive a reward rather than a share of profits, and there is no guarantee the product will ever be delivered. Consumer groups advise backers to research the creator's track record and to treat contributions as support for an idea rather than a purchase.
passages.C1P_SLEEPHISTORY: Historian Roger Ekirch has argued that before the spread of artificial lighting, people in Western Europe commonly slept in two phases: a 'first sleep' beginning soon after dusk, followed by a period of wakefulness in the middle of the night, and then a 'second sleep' until morning. During the waking interval people prayed, read, talked or visited neighbours. Ekirch suggests that some modern cases of waking in the night may be a return to this older pattern rather than a disorder.
passages.C1P_OPENOFFICE: Open-plan offices were widely adopted on the assumption that removing walls would encourage collaboration. A study conducted at two large companies, however, found that after moving to open-plan spaces, face-to-face interaction fell by around 70%, while email and messaging increased. The researchers suggested that employees, feeling observed and seeking privacy, withdrew into digital communication. The findings have prompted some firms to provide a mix of open areas and quiet rooms.
passages.C1P_CLIMATEMIGRATION: Climate change is increasingly cited as a driver of migration, yet the relationship is complex. Environmental pressures such as drought rarely act alone; they interact with poverty, conflict and political instability. Moreover, the poorest households often lack the resources to move at all, leaving them 'trapped' in vulnerable areas. Most climate-related movement is expected to occur within countries rather than across borders, a point often overlooked in public debate.
passages.C1P_FOODLABEL: Front-of-pack labels using a 'traffic light' system — red, amber and green for fat, sugar and salt — are intended to help consumers make healthier choices at a glance. Evidence suggests they do influence purchasing, particularly when shoppers are short of time. Manufacturers have also reformulated some products to avoid red labels. Critics, however, argue that the system can be misleading: a small portion of an unhealthy product may score better than a nutritious food eaten in a larger portion.
passages.C1P_ARCHIVES: Digital archives promise to preserve information indefinitely, yet digital material is in some respects more fragile than paper. File formats become obsolete, storage media degrade, and websites disappear without trace — a phenomenon sometimes called 'link rot'. Archivists warn of a potential 'digital dark age' in which future historians may find records of the early twenty-first century harder to access than those of previous centuries. Initiatives such as web archiving aim to counter this, but they can capture only a fraction of what is published online.
passages.C1P_TRUSTNEWS: Surveys indicate that trust in news media has declined in many countries, with audiences increasingly turning to social media for information. Yet trust varies considerably by outlet: public service broadcasters often enjoy higher levels of confidence than commercial or partisan sources. Some researchers argue that the decline reflects not only concerns about accuracy but also a sense that journalists are out of touch with ordinary people's concerns.
passages.C1P_WALKABLE: 'Fifteen-minute cities' are urban areas designed so that residents can reach most daily needs — shops, schools, health services and parks — within a fifteen-minute walk or cycle. Proponents argue the model reduces car dependence, improves health and strengthens local communities. The concept has, however, attracted controversy: some residents have interpreted associated traffic measures as restrictions on their freedom of movement, prompting debate about how such schemes are communicated and implemented.
passages.C1P_BIODIVERSITY: Biodiversity loss is often discussed in terms of charismatic species such as tigers and whales, but scientists stress that the decline of less visible organisms — insects, fungi and soil microbes — may have equally serious consequences. These organisms underpin processes such as decomposition, pollination and nutrient cycling on which agriculture depends. Because they are less studied, however, the scale of their decline is harder to measure, and conservation funding tends to favour species that capture public attention.
passages.C1P_GAMES: Video games have long been criticised as a waste of time or a cause of aggression, but a growing body of research presents a more nuanced picture. Certain action games appear to improve visual attention and reaction times, while puzzle and strategy games may enhance problem-solving skills. Researchers caution, however, that the benefits depend heavily on the type of game and the amount of time spent playing, and that excessive gaming can displace sleep and physical activity.
passages.C1P_RECYCLINGMYTH: Recycling is often presented as the cornerstone of environmental responsibility, yet waste experts emphasise that it ranks below reduction and reuse in the so-called waste hierarchy. Recycling still requires energy and transport, and some materials, notably many plastics, can be recycled only a limited number of times before their quality degrades. Moreover, contaminated recycling — items that are dirty or wrongly sorted — can result in entire loads being sent to landfill.
passages.C1P_MENTORING: Formal mentoring schemes pair less experienced employees with senior colleagues who offer guidance on career development. Evaluations suggest that mentees often benefit from greater confidence and faster promotion. Less widely recognised is the benefit to mentors themselves, who report gaining fresh perspectives and a deeper understanding of junior staff's challenges. Schemes appear most effective when participants have a say in who they are paired with, rather than being assigned arbitrarily.
passages.C1P_LANGUAGEAI: Machine translation has improved dramatically, and for many everyday purposes it is now remarkably accurate. Professional translators, however, point out that it still struggles with ambiguity, humour, cultural references and specialised terminology. In legal and medical contexts, where errors can have serious consequences, human review remains essential. Many translators now work as 'post-editors', correcting and refining machine output rather than translating from scratch.
passages.C1P_HERITAGEBUILDING: When a historic building is restored, conservators face a difficult choice: should they return it to its original appearance, or preserve the alterations made over the centuries, which are themselves part of its history? Many modern conservation guidelines favour minimal intervention, repairing rather than replacing, and ensuring that new work is distinguishable from old. Critics argue that this approach can leave buildings looking unfinished, whereas supporters see it as more honest.
passages.C1P_TIPPING: Tipping customs vary enormously between countries. In the United States, tips form a substantial part of many service workers' income, and failing to tip is widely regarded as rude. In Japan, by contrast, tipping is uncommon and can even cause embarrassment. In the UK, a discretionary service charge of around 12.5% is often added to restaurant bills, and recent legislation requires that tips be passed on to staff in full.
passages.C2P_MERITOCRACY: The term 'meritocracy' was coined in 1958 by the sociologist Michael Young, not as an ideal but as a warning. In his satirical book, a society that allocates positions purely on the basis of measured intelligence and effort becomes rigidly stratified, with the successful convinced that they deserve their advantages and the unsuccessful deprived of any consolation. Young was dismayed when politicians later adopted the word approvingly, apparently oblivious to its original irony. Contemporary critics echo his concern, arguing that the rhetoric of merit can obscure the role of inherited advantage and luck.
passages.C2P_TRANSLATIONPOETRY: Poetry is often said to be what gets lost in translation. Yet some of the most celebrated poems in English are themselves translations, and translators have long debated whether fidelity to literal meaning or to the music and feeling of the original should take precedence. A literal rendering may preserve sense while destroying rhythm; a freer version may capture the spirit at the cost of accuracy. Some translators resolve the dilemma by publishing parallel texts, inviting readers to triangulate between the original and its interpretation.
passages.C2P_PRIVACY: The claim that 'if you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear' is frequently invoked to justify surveillance. Critics contend that it rests on a misunderstanding of privacy, which is not merely about concealing wrongdoing but about preserving the space in which people can explore ideas, form relationships and change their minds without scrutiny. Moreover, what counts as 'something to hide' is determined not by the individual but by whoever controls the data — and may change as governments and norms change.
passages.C2P_EXPERTS: In fields characterised by rapid feedback, such as chess or firefighting, expert intuition can be remarkably reliable, because practitioners have had countless opportunities to learn which cues predict which outcomes. In contrast, in domains where feedback is delayed or ambiguous, such as long-term political forecasting, the confidence of experts often exceeds their accuracy. Psychologists therefore advise distinguishing between expertise grounded in a regular, learnable environment and mere familiarity with a subject.
passages.C2P_RUINS: The Romantic fascination with ruins reflected more than an appreciation of picturesque decay. For many eighteenth- and nineteenth-century writers and painters, crumbling abbeys and castles served as meditations on the transience of human ambition and the inevitable triumph of nature over culture. Some wealthy landowners went so far as to construct artificial ruins, or 'follies', on their estates — an apparent paradox that reveals how far the aesthetic of melancholy had become a fashionable commodity.
passages.C2P_ATTENTIONECON: In an economy saturated with information, attention has become the scarce resource. Platforms compete not primarily for users' money but for their time, and many design features — infinite scrolling, autoplay, variable rewards — are calibrated to maximise engagement. Critics argue that framing the resulting distraction as a failure of individual self-control obscures the asymmetry of power between users and companies that employ teams of behavioural scientists. Proposed remedies range from regulation of design practices to the cultivation of what some call 'digital sovereignty'.
passages.C2P_LINGUISTICS: Prescriptive grammarians lay down rules about how language ought to be used, while descriptive linguists set out to record how it is actually used. The distinction is often caricatured as a clash between pedants and relativists, but most linguists acknowledge that standard varieties serve real functions in education and formal communication. Their objection is rather to the presentation of social conventions as timeless logical laws, and to the stigmatisation of speakers of non-standard varieties as careless or unintelligent.
passages.C2P_PHILANTHROPYHISTORY: Victorian philanthropy is frequently remembered through its grand public institutions — libraries, museums and model housing estates. Yet historians note that much charitable activity at the time was conditional: aid was distributed according to judgements about the 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor, and recipients were often subjected to moral supervision. This legacy, they argue, continues to shape debates about welfare, in which the question of whether assistance should be universal or targeted remains contested.
passages.C2P_SCIENCEMETHOD: Popular accounts of science often portray discovery as a sudden flash of insight by a lone genius. Historians of science, however, emphasise the collaborative, incremental and often messy nature of research, in which failed experiments, disputes over priority and the slow accumulation of data play decisive roles. The 'eureka' narrative, they suggest, persists partly because it makes for a compelling story, but it can mislead students into believing that setbacks indicate a lack of talent rather than an ordinary feature of scientific work.
passages.C2P_CITYMEMORY: Street names are rarely neutral. They commemorate particular figures and events, and in doing so encode a version of history into the fabric of everyday life. Periods of political upheaval are frequently accompanied by waves of renaming, as new regimes seek to erase the symbols of their predecessors. Such changes can provoke fierce resistance, not only for ideological reasons but because names accumulate personal associations: for many residents, the old name is bound up with memories that have little to do with the person it honoured.
passages.C2P_NOSTALGIA: Nostalgia was once classified as a medical condition, a form of melancholy afflicting soldiers and emigrants far from home. Contemporary psychologists take a more benign view: research suggests that nostalgic reflection can bolster self-esteem, foster a sense of social connectedness and counteract loneliness. Nonetheless, nostalgia has a political dimension that is less benign, as appeals to an idealised past can be mobilised to resist change or to exclude those who do not fit a particular vision of national identity.
passages.C2P_GENTRIFICATION: Gentrification — the influx of wealthier residents into previously working-class neighbourhoods — is frequently portrayed in stark terms, either as revitalisation or as displacement. Empirical studies paint a more ambiguous picture. Long-standing residents who manage to stay may benefit from improved services and safety, yet rising rents can force out tenants, and the closure of familiar shops and gathering places can erode the social fabric even for those who remain. The policy challenge lies in capturing the benefits of investment without dispersing existing communities.
passages.C2P_HUMOUR: Humour is notoriously difficult to translate, not merely because of puns and wordplay but because it depends on shared assumptions about what is incongruous, taboo or absurd. A joke that delights one audience may baffle or offend another. Comedians who tour internationally often report rewriting material extensively, retaining the structure of a joke while replacing its cultural references — a process that resembles translation more than mere repetition.
passages.C2P_SLOWFOOD: The Slow Food movement, founded in Italy in the 1980s partly in protest against the opening of a fast-food restaurant near Rome's Spanish Steps, advocates for local, seasonal and traditionally produced food. Its proponents argue that it preserves biodiversity, supports small producers and revives culinary heritage. Detractors, however, characterise it as elitist, pointing out that artisanal products are often beyond the means of low-income households, for whom cheap, convenient food is a necessity rather than a choice.
passages.C2P_CITIZENSCIENCE: Citizen science projects, in which members of the public contribute to research by collecting or analysing data, have expanded dramatically with the spread of smartphones. Volunteers classify galaxies, count birds and record the timing of spring flowering, generating datasets far larger than professional scientists could gather alone. Concerns about data quality persist, but studies indicate that with appropriate training and statistical correction, volunteer data can match professional standards. Participants, meanwhile, report greater scientific literacy and engagement.
passages.C2P_CLASSICS: The study of Greek and Latin, once the cornerstone of an elite British education, has declined markedly in state schools. Advocates of the classics argue that the subjects cultivate analytical rigour, enrich understanding of English vocabulary and illuminate the foundations of Western thought. Critics counter that the curriculum has historically reinforced social hierarchies. Recent initiatives seek to reconcile these positions by introducing classical languages in state primary schools, presenting them as a resource for all rather than a marker of privilege.
